claims.statement: The article's aggregate runner work metric is an execution-work comparison, not a billed-minutes or cost claim; GitHub exposes billing/usage under separate rules and public standard GitHub-hosted repository usage is not billed like private-repository minutes.

evidence.relevance: GitHub documents job execution time separately from billable job execution minutes and states where billable-minute details are exposed.
GitHub documents Actions billing/usage as a separate accounting surface and distinguishes public standard-hosted usage from billed private-repository usage.

claims.counterEvidenceReview: Reviewed current GitHub Actions execution-time and billing/usage documentation; no basis was found for equating the article's summed observed job elapsed time with billed minutes or cost.

claims.statement: In oxide-batch's controlled four-way-versus-one-runner integration experiment, four-way execution reduced critical integration wall time by 56.73–62.48% with a 61.21% median while increasing aggregate integration work by 24.94–51.37% with a 41.45% median, under the same source SHA, target denominator, toolchain, runner architecture and protected-main read-only cache policy.

evidence.relevance: The final public checkpoint records the completed 2x A-to-B plus 2x B-to-A evidence, exact comparison controls, wall-time reduction range/median and aggregate-work overhead range/median.
The public measurement owner defines the exact-cover, same-toolchain, same-runner, same-cache proof obligations and explicitly excludes billing claims or production topology changes.

claims.counterEvidenceReview: Reviewed the final measurement checkpoint and experiment contract, including invalid/non-authoritative boundaries; no contradictory authoritative pair was found.

claims.statement: In oxide-batch's controlled three-lane-versus-current-four-lane crossover, the three-lane candidate reduced summed core execution by a median 10.94% and summed lane-job elapsed by 12.41%, but increased core critical latency by 18.89% and lane-job critical latency by 16.61%; all four valid pairs agreed in direction and the repository kept the current four-way topology.

evidence.relevance: The final topology disposition records the 2x A4-to-C3 plus 2x C3-to-A4 crossover, all four paired deltas, medians and KEEP CURRENT 4-WAY / C3 NO-GO decision.
The closure checkpoint confirms the research-complete KEEP_CURRENT_4_WAY disposition and that no production shard-count/cache-policy mutation was made by the research closeout.

claims.counterEvidenceReview: Reviewed the final crossover evidence and closure record as well as earlier reuse candidates; none met both latency and aggregate-work objectives, and no contrary authoritative C3 pair was found.

claims.statement: The mold results are topology-specific rather than repository-wide: oxide-batch's October x86_64 cold experiment had only +0.09% paired-mean saving and was rejected; ARM64 plus steady-state sccache later measured 56.331s system versus 52.207s mold, a 7.32% mean-of-times saving with mold faster in 4/4 pairs and scoped adoption; current x86_64 plus warm sccache measured 64.283s versus 64.266s, about 0.028% with mold faster in only 1/4 pairs and remained rejected. Arkst similarly moved from an October x86_64 cold result where mold was 1.38% slower to an ARM64 steady-state result of 175.514s versus 116.546s, a 33.60% job-local saving in 4/4 pairs, while explicitly not claiming a 33.6% repository-wide Merge Gate improvement.

claims.statement: For CI optimization decisions like those in this article, choose the target metric before optimizing, hold the validation denominator and comparison conditions explicit, retain NO-GO evidence, re-measure when runner/cache/workload topology materially changes, and keep controlled causal A/B evidence separate from post-adoption operational observations; policy relaxation or validation-scope changes should be classified separately from making the same validation faster.

evidence.relevance: The four-way experiment demonstrates a measured latency-versus-aggregate-work trade-off under a fixed validation denominator and explicitly avoids billing/generalization claims.
The three-lane follow-up shows why reducing aggregate work alone was insufficient when critical latency regressed consistently.
The current x86_64 re-evaluation preserves a NO-GO despite ARM64 adoption, demonstrating architecture/topology-specific decisions.
The Arkst ARM64 re-evaluation documents why a changed high-hit cache topology justified re-measuring an old reject and explicitly limits the result to job-local scope.

claims.counterEvidenceReview: Adversarially reviewed the experiments for cases where one metric could substitute for another or where a production observation could be mistaken for causal A/B evidence. The public records instead reinforce the bounded, topology-specific decision model and contain explicit non-generalization clauses.

conditions: The optimization is being evaluated against an explicit CI objective such as developer-visible latency, critical-path latency, aggregate runner work or a bounded job-local metric.
Validation scope, source/toolchain identity and runner/cache conditions can be held constant or their differences can be explicitly classified.
Production observations are used to validate operational survival, not to manufacture an uncontrolled causal percentage.
alternatives: Optimize only one explicitly declared local metric and avoid making repository-wide claims when critical-path or aggregate-work evidence is unavailable.
Treat validation-scope, security-policy or scheduling changes as separate engineering decisions rather than counting them as same-scope performance wins.
Keep the current topology when controlled evidence does not show a worthwhile trade-off, and re-open the decision only after a material topology change.

crossClaimConsistency.summary: Verified that job-local mold gains are not rewritten as repository-wide Merge Gate gains, aggregate runner work is not rewritten as billing cost, sharding keeps the same validation denominator, x86_64 negative evidence remains visible beside ARM64 adoption, and production observations do not replace controlled A/B claims.

adversarialReview.summary: A fresh adversarial pass challenged the 61.21% sharding latency result, the 33.60% Arkst mold result, the claim that four-way remains justified, the production follow-up samples and the final decision model. The final text preserves the aggregate-work cost, critical-path caveat, architecture-specific rejects, uncontrolled-production limitation and validation-scope boundary.
